concepts.title: Kingdoms after the Mauryas
concepts.definition: After the Mauryas, the subcontinent was reorganised into many kingdoms: Shaka and Kushana rulers from Central Asia, Satavahanas in the Deccan, and others who adopted Indian ways even as they arrived.
concepts.key_idea: Political break-up did not mean cultural break: new rulers settled in and joined the civilisation they entered.

concepts.title: Trade Routes: Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha
concepts.definition: Highways reorganised commerce: the Uttarapatha ran across the north, the Dakshinapatha pierced the Deccan to the southern ports, and both carried goods between land and sea routes to Rome and Southeast Asia.
concepts.key_idea: Roads are arteries of civilisation: along the routes moved cloth, spices, coins, monks and ideas.

concepts.title: A Living Tradition of Change
concepts.definition: The chapter opens with the thought that by a continuous living tradition and vital power of rejuvenescence, this land readjusted itself through unnumbered transformations; each new wave was absorbed and made Indian.
concepts.key_idea: India's strength is renewal: change after change left the civilisation itself alive and growing.

concepts.title: Legacy of the Age of Reorganisation
concepts.definition: The age left a legacy of devotional religion, Gandhara and Mathura art, Sanskrit literature and science, coinage and trade networks that later ages, including the Guptas, built upon.
concepts.key_idea: What looks like a pause between empires is a workshop: the reorganisation age forged the tools of the golden age to come.
